# Rust, embedded

The shortest path: depend on `patala-core`, program against `PaymentRail`,
and add rail crates as you need them. No boundary, no second process, no
generated wrapper, native types throughout.

## Dependencies

patala is not on crates.io yet — v0.1.1 is tagged, but no workflow builds or
publishes anything from a tag (`SECURITY.md`).
Vendor by path or by git:

```toml
[dependencies]
patala-core = { git = "https://github.com/vul-os/patala" }

# Opt in per rail. None of these are pulled in unless you name them —
# see docs/offline-by-default.md for why that is structural, not incidental.
patala-stellar = { git = "https://github.com/vul-os/patala" }
patala-fiat    = { git = "https://github.com/vul-os/patala", features = ["stripe"] }
```

`patala-core` depends on nothing but `async-trait`, `serde`, `serde_json` and
`thiserror` — 12 crates in total, measured with `cargo tree -e normal`. Real
rails depend on `patala-core`, never the reverse, which is what keeps that
number from drifting.

## The whole surface

Seven methods, and you will use four of them most of the time:

```rust
use patala_core::{MockRail, PayRequest, PaymentRail, RailClass};

let rail = MockRail::new("mock", RailClass::NonCustodialFinal, vec!["USDC".into()]);

let req = PayRequest {
    amount_minor: 500, // 5.00 USDC — integer minor units, never a float
    currency: "USDC".into(),
    destination: "wallet-or-processor-token".into(),
    reference: "order-1".into(),
};

let receipt = rail.charge(&req).await.unwrap();
assert_eq!(receipt.reference, "order-1");
assert!(rail.verify(&receipt).await.unwrap());
```

`rail.id()` and `rail.capabilities()` are synchronous and free;
`quote`, `charge`, `verify`, `refund` and `verify_webhook` are `async`;
`validate_destination` is synchronous, pure and offline — safe to call on
every keystroke of an address field.

## Failover, and the guard on it

`FailoverRail` wraps `Vec<Box<dyn PaymentRail>>` and tries them in order,
falling through on error. It lives in the substrate rather than in a gateway,
so every self-hoster gets it:

```rust
use patala_core::{FailoverRail, MockRail, PayRequest, PaymentRail, RailClass};

let primary = MockRail::new("solana-mock", RailClass::NonCustodialFinal, vec!["USDC".into()]);
let backup  = MockRail::new("stellar-mock", RailClass::NonCustodialFinal, vec!["USDC".into()]);
let rail = FailoverRail::new(vec![Box::new(primary), Box::new(backup)]);

let req = PayRequest {
    amount_minor: 1_500,
    currency: "USDC".into(),
    destination: "wallet-address-or-processor-token".into(),
    reference: "order-42".into(),
};

let receipt = rail.charge(&req).await.unwrap();
assert!(rail.verify(&receipt).await.unwrap());
```

It will **not** silently fall from a `NonCustodialFinal` request onto a
`CustodialReversible` rail, or the reverse. That is not a conservative default
you should switch off casually — it changes the guarantee you handed the
payer. If you genuinely mean it, say so:

```rust
let rail = FailoverRail::new(rails).allow_cross_class(true);
```

Crossing the class boundary trips `Error::CrossClassFailover` otherwise, and
every rail failing gives `Error::AllRailsFailed`.

## The types you will actually touch

| Type | Shape | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `PayRequest` | `amount_minor: u64`, `currency: String`, `destination: String`, `reference: String` | Integer minor units, always. `PayRequest::validate()` requires a non-empty destination. |
| `Quote` | fees, FX, expiry | `total_minor` is a `u64`. |
| `Receipt` | `rail_id`, `reference`, `amount_minor`, `proof` | `proof` is the rail's binding data. Store it; `verify` re-derives from it. |
| `RailCapabilities` | `class`, `reversible`, `requires_kyc`, `holds_funds`, `currencies`, `settlement`, `atomic_multi_party` | Everything you may know about a rail without naming its provider. |
| `Error` | `Unsupported`, `Rail`, `InvalidRequest`, `CrossClassFailover`, `AllRailsFailed` | |

`verify` returning `Ok(false)` is the fail-closed *answer*, never an error.
`Err` means the check could not be performed at all — a different thing, and
you should treat it as such.

## What only Rust can reach

Because [everything non-Rust dispatches through `dyn PaymentRail`](polyglot.md),
inherent methods that are not on the trait are Rust-only. There is one that
matters in practice:

- **`ManualRail::mark_paid` / `mark_failed`** — the "bank transfer, an operator
  confirms it later" flow. `charge()` on the manual rail returns instructions
  and `amount_minor: 0`, and stays honestly unpaid until one of those is
  called. They are not trait methods because not every rail has an operator,
  and the consequence — unreachable from Python, Go and HTTP — is documented
  rather than worked around.

If your flow needs the manual rail to actually settle, that part of it has to
be Rust. That is a genuine constraint on
[choosing a mode](choosing-a-mode.md).

## Concurrency and runtime

patala starts nothing. There is no background task, no connection pool you did
not ask for, no runtime installed at load. The trait's methods are `async` and
run on **your** executor. A `MockRail` is `Send + Sync` and cheap to clone
behind an `Arc`; rails that hold a network client hold exactly one.

The lazily-created Tokio runtime described elsewhere in these docs belongs to
`patala-py`, so that Python callers do not have to run an event loop. It does
not exist in a Rust consumer.

## Testing your integration

Build the whole payment path against `MockRail` before you have credentials
for anything. It is deterministic, needs no network, and can be made to fail
on demand.

```bash
cargo test -p patala-core
```

For the payout-address branch of a UI, `MockRail` speaks a synthetic
`<network>:<kind>:<label>` destination grammar — deliberately not any real
chain's format — that can produce **all five** `DestinationStatus` verdicts, so
every branch is reachable with no chain in sight.
`MockRail::without_destination_checks` answers `Unknown` for everything, which
is the fiat-shaped "a human must decide" path.

One honesty note carried over from the crate: `MockRail`'s "signature" is a
small keyed digest built with `std` only. It is not a cryptographic primitive
and is not trying to be one — it exists so `verify` round-trips a genuine
receipt and rejects a mutated one, offline.
